en: The Sutra on the Elder’s Son’s Distress in Three Places, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Monastery, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a great elder in the city of Śrāvastī whose wealth was beyond measure; his fields, houses, oxen, and horses were beyond calculation, yet in his home he had no son of his own.
According to the customs of that country, if one dies without a son, their property reverts to the state after their life ends.
The elder and his wife prayed to various deities, the sun, the moon, and the stars, seeking offspring to establish their lineage, yet they were unable to obtain any.
At that time, the elder’s wife took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts; she practiced with diligence morning and night, never daring to be indolent, and soon became pregnant.
A wise woman should be known to possess five qualities:
first, she knows her husband’s intentions.
Second, she knows whether her husband’s thoughts are affectionate or not;
third, she knows the cause by which she conceived the fetus;
fourth, she distinguishes between male and female.
Fifth, distinguishing between good and evil:
this wife of the elder addressed the elder, saying,
"I am already pregnant."
The elder was filled with joy and daily provided him with clothing and food and drink of the finest quality.
When the ten months were complete, he gave birth to a son, whom five nurses attended:
one for breastfeeding, one for feeding solid food, one for bathing, one for dressing, and one for holding.
The boy grew up, reaching the age of fifteen or sixteen; the elder couple then sought a wife for their son.
They found the daughter of another elder, who was upright, beautiful, and excellent.

In a garden pavilion outside the city, he hosted a grand banquet for his guests, providing food, drink, and entertainment with exquisite delicacies; those who came from the four quarters were never turned away.
Thus, with such an entourage, seven days passed.
At that time, the boy’s parents were strolling in the garden when they came upon a tree named Aśoka; upon it were flowers of an exceedingly brilliant hue, like the color of pale vermilion.
The wife said to her husband, "I wish to have these flowers.
The husband then climbed the tree to gather them for her; however, the branches were thin and weak, and they immediately snapped, causing the child to fall to the ground, where he died instantly.

When his parents heard this, they knew he had fallen from the tree and died; they rushed toward him, the mother embracing his head and the father embracing his two feet, rubbing and gazing at him as he remained forever unconscious and did not revive.
The parents were filled with grief, their innermost being shattered; when the guests saw this, they too shared in their sorrow and pain:
"How sudden and swift was the death! While the guests' feasting and entertainment had not yet concluded, he has instead fallen from the tree and died—how impermanent is life!"

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, together with Ānanda, donned his robes and took up his alms bowl to enter the city for alms. There he saw an elder and his wife, who had only one son, fallen from a tree and died; they were weeping and grieving in a manner beyond description.

The Buddha saw where this child had come from: his life span having ended in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he was reborn in the house of an elder; upon dying there, he was reborn among the nāgas, and was then taken and eaten by a garuḍa king. Thus, in these three places, there was sorrow, and all together they held a funeral for him.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go to the householder’s place and explain the matter to him to remove his affliction;
if you do not do so, I fear he will die of grief."
Ānanda replied, “So be it!
and immediately followed the Buddha to the householder’s residence.
When the elder heard that the Buddha had arrived at his place, his heart was immediately filled with joy, and he prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet.
The Buddha asked the elder,
"Why are you so sorrowful and distressed?"
The householder said to the Buddha:

“I am without merit; it was only because I had one son that I sought a wife for him, invited guests for a meal, and provided entertainment. Before these festivities were finished, he climbed a tree to gather flowers, fell to the ground, and died.”
"My body is like stone and my heart is as hard as tempered iron; having just obtained this one son, he has abandoned me and died.
The Buddha told the elder:
"In the life of man there is death; when things are formed, they must decay. When the opposing conditions arrive and life reaches its end, it cannot be avoided or hidden."
"Cast away your anxieties; do not grieve any longer.
At that time, the Buddha emitted a radiance that illuminated the ten directions, causing the elder to see his parents among the devas and nāgas weeping.
The Buddha said to the elder:

"This child originally had his lifespan exhausted and his life ended in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whereupon he was reborn in your household. When his lifespan there was exhausted, he was reborn among the dragons, and the King of the Garuḍas immediately seized him to devour him. Since they are all weeping simultaneously in these three places, whose son is he?"
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Are you one of the sons of the devas in the heavens?
Or are you among the nāgas, the son of a nāga deity?”
Then the Buddha himself explained, saying:
"They are not these sons of devas, nor are they your sons, O King, nor are they the sons of nāgas."
"The various causes and conditions of birth and death are impermanent, like an illusion;
nothing endures for long, being like a passing traveler.
The Buddha said to the elder:
"Death cannot be avoided; once one has departed, nothing follows.
The elder addressed the Buddha, saying, "What were the karmic merits and faults of this child in his past lives?"
“Born into a family of great wealth yet meeting with an early death—what is the karmic response for this?
The Buddha said, “In a previous life, this child delighted in practicing generosity and honored others; by virtue of this merit, he was born into a family of great wealth.”
One who delights in the sport of hunting and harms living beings will, for this reason, have a short life.
Sin and merit follow a person just as a shadow follows a form.
The elder leaped for joy and attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
When the Buddha had thus spoken, the elder and his wife, along with the entire assembly, received it with great joy.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Elder’s Son’s Distress in Three Places.
